37: The Python SDK makes it easy to capture events, evaluate feature flags, track errors, and more in your Python apps.
38: 
39: > These docs cover version `7.x` of the Python SDK, which requires Python 3.10 or higher. On Python 3.9? See [supported versions](#supported-versions).
40: 
41: ## Installation
42: 
43: ```bash
44: pip install posthog
45: ```
46: 
47: **Upgrading to v6**
48: 
49: Version `6.x` of the PostHog Python SDK introduces a new [contexts](https://posthog.com/docs/libraries/python.md#contexts) API and breaking changes. If you're upgrading from `5.x` to `6.x`, read the [migration guide](https://posthog.com/tutorials/python-v6-migration.md) first to learn more.
50: 
51: In your app, import the `posthog` library and set your project token and host **before** making any calls.
52: 
53: ```python
54: from posthog import Posthog
55: 
56: posthog = Posthog('<ph_project_token>', host='https://us.i.posthog.com')
57: ```
58: 
59: > **Note:** As a rule of thumb, we do not recommend having API keys or tokens in plaintext. Setting it as an environment variable is best.
60: 
61: You can find your project token and instance address in the [project settings](https://app.posthog.com/project/settings) page in PostHog.
62: 
63: ## Use the asyncio client
64: 
65: The Python SDK includes an asyncio-native client in version `7.45.0` and later. Continue to use `Posthog` in synchronous apps. For an asyncio app, install the optional async dependencies:
66: 
67: ```bash
68: pip install "posthog[async]>=7.45.0"
69: ```
70: 
71: Import `AsyncPosthog`, the customer-facing name for `AsyncClient`. Both names provide the same async context manager and lifecycle methods. Keep one client for the lifetime of your app. For example, use a FastAPI lifespan handler:
72: 
73: ```python
74: import os
75: from contextlib import asynccontextmanager
76: 
77: from fastapi import FastAPI
78: from posthog import AsyncPosthog
79: 
80: @asynccontextmanager
81: async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):
82:     async with AsyncPosthog(
83:         os.environ["POSTHOG_PROJECT_TOKEN"],
84:         host=os.environ["POSTHOG_HOST"],
85:         secret_key=os.environ.get("POSTHOG_FEATURE_FLAGS_SECURE_API_KEY"),
86:     ) as posthog:
87:         app.state.posthog = posthog
88:         yield
89: 
90: app = FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan)
91: ```
92: 
93: Exiting the context calls `shutdown()`. This flushes buffered events, waits for in-flight operations, stops the workers, and closes the HTTP transport. If you don't use the context manager, call `await posthog.shutdown()` during app shutdown. `await posthog.join()` has the same effect.
94: 
95: ### Capture events without blocking the event loop
96: 
97: `capture()` queues an event and returns without waiting for a network request. Don't await it:
98: 
99: ```python
100: posthog.capture(
101:     "event_name",
102:     distinct_id="user-distinct-id",
103:     properties={"source": "fastapi"},
104: )
105: ```
106: 
107: Use `capture_immediate()` when your code must wait for that event's delivery attempt:
108: 
109: ```python
110: capture_id = await posthog.capture_immediate(
111:     "event_name",
112:     distinct_id="user-distinct-id",
113: )
114: ```
115: 
116: ### Evaluate feature flags
117: 
118: Await `evaluate_flags()` once, then use its snapshot with synchronous in-memory accessors. Pass the same snapshot to `capture()` to attach the exact values used for branching without another feature flag request:
119: 
120: ```python
121: flags = await posthog.evaluate_flags("user-distinct-id")
122: 
123: if flags.is_enabled("new-checkout"):
124:     # Show the new checkout
125:     pass
126: 
127: posthog.capture(
128:     "checkout started",
129:     distinct_id="user-distinct-id",
130:     flags=flags,
131: )
132: ```
133: 
134: The snapshot provides synchronous `is_enabled()`, `get_flag()`, and `get_flag_payload()` accessors. The awaited `evaluate_flags()` call also accepts `groups`, `person_properties`, `group_properties`, `disable_geoip`, `flag_keys`, and `device_id` arguments.
135: 
136: ### Fetch remote config
137: 
138: Initialize the client with a server-side [secret API key](https://posthog.com/docs/feature-flags/remote-config.md#step-1-get-a-secret-api-key) as `secret_key`, then await the remote config request:
139: 
140: ```python
141: config = await posthog.get_remote_config_payload("landing-page-config")
142: ```
143: 
144: See [Remote config](https://posthog.com/docs/feature-flags/remote-config.md) for setup and security details.
145: 
146: ## Identifying users
147: 
148: > **Identifying users is required.** Backend events need a `distinct_id` to associate events with the correct user.
149: >
150: > In Python, you can do this through a context. All event captures in the same context will be tagged automatically with the correct `distinct_id`. Typically, you would set a fresh context and identify at the top of each route.
151: >
152: > ```python
153: > from posthog import new_context, identify_context, capture
154: >
155: > @app.get("/foo")
156: > def foo(current_user: User = Depends(get_current_user)):
157: >     with new_context(): # Set context at the top of a route
158: >         identify_context(current_user.id)
159: >         capture("foo_viewed")
160: >     return {"status": "ok"}
161: > ```
162: >
163: > When possible, write a small piece of **middleware** that resolves your authenticated user, wrap a context around the request, and identifies it. Every `capture()` downstream is then attributed *automatically*. The SDK's Django middleware does this automatically and you can replicate it when using the plain Python SDK.
164: 
165: ## Capturing events
166: 
167: You can send custom events using `capture`:
168: 
169: ```python
170: # Events captured with no context or explicit distinct_id are marked as personless and have an auto-generated distinct_id:
171: posthog.capture('some-anon-event')
172: 
173: from posthog import identify_context, new_context
174: 
175: # Use contexts to manage user identification across multiple capture calls
176: with new_context():
177:     identify_context('distinct_id_of_the_user')
178:     posthog.capture('user_signed_up')
179:     posthog.capture('user_logged_in')
180:     # You can also capture events with a specific distinct_id
181:     posthog.capture('some-custom-action', distinct_id='distinct_id_of_the_user')
182: ```
183: 
184: > **Tip:** We recommend using a `[object] [verb]` format for your event names, where `[object]` is the entity that the behavior relates to, and `[verb]` is the behavior itself. For example, `project created`, `user signed up`, or `invite sent`.
185: 
186: > **Tip:** You can define event schemas with typed properties and generate type-safe code using [schema management](https://posthog.com/docs/product-analytics/schema-management.md).
187: 
188: ### Setting event properties
189: 
190: Optionally, you can include additional information with the event by including a [properties](https://posthog.com/docs/data/events.md#event-properties) object:
191: 
192: ```python
193: posthog.capture(
194:     "user_signed_up",
195:     distinct_id="distinct_id_of_the_user",
196:     properties={
197:         "login_type": "email",
198:         "is_free_trial": "true"
199:     }
200: )
201: ```
202: 
203: ### Sending page views
204: 
205: If you're aiming for a backend-only implementation of PostHog and won't be capturing events from your frontend, you can send `pageviews` from your backend like so:
206: 
207: ```python
208: posthog.capture('$pageview', distinct_id="distinct_id_of_the_user", properties={'$current_url': 'https://example.com'})
209: ```
210: 
211: ## Person profiles and properties
212: 
213: The Python SDK captures identified events if the current context is identified or if you pass a distinct ID explicitly. These create [person profiles](https://posthog.com/docs/data/persons.md). To set [person properties](https://posthog.com/docs/product-analytics/person-properties.md) in these profiles, include them when capturing an event:
214: 
215: ```python
216: # Passing a distinct id explicitly
217: posthog.capture(
218:     'event_name',
219:     distinct_id='user-distinct-id',
220:     properties={
221:         '$set': {'name': 'Max Hedgehog'},
222:         '$set_once': {'initial_url': '/blog'}
223:     }
224: )
225: 
226: # Using contexts
227: from posthog import new_context, identify_context
228: with new_context():
229:     identify_context('user-distinct-id')
230:     posthog.capture('event_name')
231: ```
232: 
233: For more details on the difference between `$set` and `$set_once`, see our [person properties docs](https://posthog.com/docs/product-analytics/person-properties.md#what-is-the-difference-between-set-and-set_once).
234: 
235: To capture [anonymous events](https://posthog.com/docs/data/anonymous-vs-identified-events.md) without person profiles, set the event's `$process_person_profile` property to `False`. Events captured with no context or explicit distinct\_id are marked as personless, and will have an auto-generated distinct\_id:
236: 
237: ```python
238: posthog.capture(
239:     event='event_name',
240:     properties={
241:         '$process_person_profile': False
242:     }
243: )
244: ```
245: 
246: ## Alias
247: 
248: Sometimes, you want to assign multiple distinct IDs to a single user. This is helpful when your primary distinct ID is inaccessible. For example, if a distinct ID used on the frontend is not available in your backend.
249: 
250: In this case, you can use `alias` to assign another distinct ID to the same user.
251: 
252: ```python
253: posthog.alias(previous_id='distinct_id', distinct_id='alias_id')
254: ```
255: 
256: We strongly recommend reading our docs on [alias](https://posthog.com/docs/product-analytics/identify.md#alias-assigning-multiple-distinct-ids-to-the-same-user) to best understand how to correctly use this method.
257: 
258: ## Contexts
259: 
260: The Python SDK uses nested contexts for managing state that's shared across events. Contexts are the recommended way to manage things like "which user is taking this action" (through `identify_context`), rather than manually passing user state through your apps stack.
261: 
262: When events (including exceptions) are captured in a context, the event uses the user [distinct ID](https://posthog.com/docs/getting-started/identify-users.md), [session ID](https://posthog.com/docs/data/sessions.md), and tags that are (optionally) set in the context. This is useful for adding properties to multiple events during a single user's interaction with your product.
263: 
264: You can enter a context using the `with` statement:
265: 
266: ```python
267: from posthog import new_context, tag, set_context_session, identify_context
268: 
269: with new_context():
270:     tag("transaction_id", "abc123")
271:     tag("some_arbitrary_value", {"tags": "can be dicts"})
272: 
273:     # Sessions are UUIDv7 values and used to track a sequence of events that occur within a single user session
274:     # See https://posthog.com/docs/data/sessions
275:     set_context_session(session_id)
276: 
277:     # Setting the context-level distinct ID. See below for more details.
278:     identify_context(user_id)
279: 
280:     # This event is captured with the distinct ID, session ID, and tags set above
281:     posthog.capture("order_processed")
282: ```
283: 
284: Contexts are persisted across function calls. If you enter one and then call a function and capture an event in the called function, it uses the context tags and session ID set in the parent context:
285: 
286: ```python
287: from posthog import new_context, tag
288: 
289: def some_function():
290:     # When called from `outer_function`, this event is captured with the property some-key="value-4"
291:     posthog.capture("order_processed")
292: 
293: 
294: def outer_function():
295:     with new_context():
296:         tag("some-key", "value-4")
297:         some_function()
298: ```
299: 
300: Contexts are nested, so tags added to a parent context are inherited by child contexts. If you set the same tag in both a parent and child context, the child context's value overrides the parent's at event capture (but the parent context won't be affected). This nesting also applies to session IDs and distinct IDs.
301: 
302: ```python
303: from posthog import new_context, tag
304: 
305: with new_context():
306:     tag("some-key", "value-1")
307:     tag("some-other-key", "another-value")
308:     with new_context():
309:         tag("some-key", "value-2")
310:         # This event is captured with some-key="value-2" and some-other-key="another-value"
311:         posthog.capture("order_processed")
312: 
313:     # This event is captured with some-key="value-1" and some-other-key="another-value"
314:     posthog.capture("order_processed")
315: ```
316: 
317: You can disable this nesting behavior by passing `fresh=True` to `new_context`:
318: 
319: ```python
320: from posthog import new_context, tag
321: 
322: with new_context(fresh=True):
323:     tag("some-key", "value-2")
324:     # This event only has the property some-key="value-2" from the fresh context
325:     posthog.capture("order_processed")
326: ```
327: 
328: > **Note:** Distinct IDs, session IDs, and properties passed directly to calls to `capture` and related functions override context state in the final event captured.
329: 
330: ### Contexts and user identification
331: 
332: Contexts can be associated with a distinct ID by calling `posthog.identify_context`:
333: 
334: ```python
335: from posthog import identify_context
336: 
337: identify_context("distinct-id")
338: ```
339: 
340: Within a context associated with a distinct ID, all events captured are associated with that user. You can override the distinct ID for a specific event by passing a `distinct_id` argument to `capture`:
341: 
342: ```python
343: from posthog import new_context, identify_context
344: 
345: with new_context():
346:     identify_context("distinct-id")
347:     posthog.capture("order_processed") # will be associated with distinct-id
348:     posthog.capture("order_processed", distinct_id="another-distinct-id") # will be associated with another-distinct-id
349: ```
350: 
351: It's recommended to pass the currently active distinct ID from the frontend to the backend, using the `X-POSTHOG-DISTINCT-ID` header. If you're using our Django middleware, this is extracted and associated with the request handler context automatically.
352: 
353: You can read more about identifying users in the [user identification documentation](https://posthog.com/docs/product-analytics/identify.md).
354: 
355: ### Contexts and sessions
356: 
357: Contexts can be associated with a session ID by calling `posthog.set_context_session`. When linking backend events to frontend sessions, use the session ID from the frontend SDK (PostHog session IDs are UUIDv7 strings).
358: 
359: ```python
360: from posthog import new_context, set_context_session
361: with new_context():
362:     set_context_session(request.get_header("X-POSTHOG-SESSION-ID"))
363: ```
364: 
365: **Using PostHog on your frontend too?**
366: 
367: If you're using the PostHog JavaScript Web SDK on your frontend, it generates a session ID for you. Configure [`tracing_headers`](https://posthog.com/docs/libraries/js/config.md#tracing-headers) for your backend hostname to add the session and distinct ID headers to browser requests automatically.
368: 
369: You need to extract the header in your request handler (if you're using our Django middleware integration, this happens automatically).
370: 
371: If you associate a context with a session, you'll be able to do things like:
372: 
373: -   See backend events on the session timeline when viewing session replays
374: -   View session replays for users that triggered a backend exception in error tracking
375: 
376: You can read more about sessions in the [session tracking](https://posthog.com/docs/data/sessions.md) documentation.
377: 
378: ### Exception capture
379: 
380: By default exceptions raised within a context are captured and available in the [error tracking](https://posthog.com/docs/error-tracking.md) dashboard. You can override this behavior by passing `capture_exceptions=False` to `new_context`:
381: 
382: ```python
383: from posthog import new_context, tag
384: 
385: with new_context(capture_exceptions=False):
386:     tag("transaction_id", "abc123")
387:     tag("some_arbitrary_value", {"tags": "can be dicts"})
388: 
389:     # This event will be captured with the tags set above
390:     posthog.capture("order_processed")
391:     # This exception will not be captured
392:     raise Exception("Order processing failed")
393: ```
394: 
395: ### Decorating functions
396: 
397: The SDK exposes a function decorator. It takes the same `fresh` and `capture_exceptions` arguments as `new_context` and provides a handy way to mark a whole function as being in a new context. For example:
398: 
399: ```python
400: from posthog import scoped, identify_context
401: 
402: @scoped(fresh=True)
403: def process_order(user, order_id):
404:     identify_context(user.distinct_id)
405:     posthog.capture("order_processed") # Associated with the user
406:     raise Exception("Order processing failed") # This exception is also captured and associated with the user
407: ```

409: ## Group analytics
410: 
411: Group analytics allows you to associate an event with a group (e.g. teams, organizations, etc.). Read the [Group Analytics](https://posthog.com/docs/user-guides/group-analytics.md) guide for more information.
412: 
413: > **Note:** This is a paid feature and is not available on the open-source or free cloud plan. Learn more on our [pricing page](https://posthog.com/pricing.md).
414: 
415: To capture an event and associate it with a group:
416: 
417: ```python
418: posthog.capture('some_event', groups={'company': 'company_id_in_your_db'})
419: ```
420: 
421: To update properties on a group:
422: 
423: ```python
424: posthog.group_identify('company', 'company_id_in_your_db', {
425:     'name': 'Awesome Inc.',
426:     'employees': 11
427: })
428: ```
429: 
430: The `name` is a special property which is used in the PostHog UI for the name of the group. If you don't specify a `name` property, the group ID will be used instead.

432: ## Feature flags
433: 
434: The examples in this section use the synchronous `Posthog` client. For `AsyncPosthog`, use the [awaited feature flag example](#evaluate-feature-flags). The returned snapshot uses the same accessors.
435: 
436: PostHog's [feature flags](https://posthog.com/docs/feature-flags.md) enable you to safely deploy and roll back new features as well as target specific users and groups with them.
437: 
438: There are two steps to implement feature flags in Python:
439: 
440: ### Step 1: Evaluate flags once
441: 
442: Call `posthog.evaluate_flags()` once for the user, then read values from the returned snapshot.
443: 
444: #### Boolean feature flags
445: 
446: ```python
447: flags = posthog.evaluate_flags("distinct_id_of_your_user")
448: 
449: if flags.is_enabled("flag-key"):
450:     # Do something differently for this user
451:     # Optional: fetch the payload
452:     matched_flag_payload = flags.get_flag_payload("flag-key")
453: ```
454: 
455: #### Multivariate feature flags
456: 
457: ```python
458: flags = posthog.evaluate_flags("distinct_id_of_your_user")
459: 
460: enabled_variant = flags.get_flag("flag-key")
461: 
462: if enabled_variant == "variant-key":  # replace "variant-key" with the key of your variant
463:     # Do something differently for this user
464:     # Optional: fetch the payload
465:     matched_flag_payload = flags.get_flag_payload("flag-key")
466: ```
467: 
468: `flags.get_flag()` returns the variant string for multivariate flags, `True` for enabled boolean flags, `False` for disabled flags, and `None` when the flag wasn't returned by the evaluation.
469: 
470: > **Note:** `posthog.feature_enabled()`, `posthog.get_feature_flag()`, `posthog.get_feature_flag_payload()`, and `posthog.capture(send_feature_flags=True)` still work during the migration period, but they're deprecated. Prefer `posthog.evaluate_flags()` for new code.
471: 
472: ### Step 2: Include feature flag information when capturing events
473: 
474: If you want use your feature flag to breakdown or filter events in your [insights](https://posthog.com/docs/product-analytics/insights.md), you'll need to include feature flag information in those events. This ensures that the feature flag value is attributed correctly to the event.
475: 
476: > **Note:** This step is only required for events captured using our server-side SDKs or [API](https://posthog.com/docs/api.md).
477: 
478: There are two methods you can use to include feature flag information in your events:
479: 
480: #### Method 1: Pass the evaluated flags snapshot to `capture()`
481: 
482: Pass the same `flags` object that you used for branching. This attaches the exact flag values from that evaluation and doesn't make another `/flags` request.
483: 
484: ```python
485: flags = posthog.evaluate_flags("distinct_id_of_your_user")
486: 
487: if flags.is_enabled("flag-key"):
488:     # Do something differently for this user
489:     pass
490: 
491: posthog.capture(
492:     "event_name",
493:     distinct_id="distinct_id_of_your_user",
494:     flags=flags,
495: )
496: ```
497: 
498: By default, this attaches every flag in the snapshot using `$feature/<flag-key>` properties and `$active_feature_flags`.
499: 
500: To reduce event property bloat, pass a filtered snapshot:
501: 
502: ```python
503: # Attach only flags accessed with is_enabled() or get_flag() before this call
504: posthog.capture(
505:     "event_name",
506:     distinct_id="distinct_id_of_your_user",
507:     flags=flags.only_accessed(),
508: )
509: 
510: # Attach only specific flags
511: posthog.capture(
512:     "event_name",
513:     distinct_id="distinct_id_of_your_user",
514:     flags=flags.only(["checkout-flow", "new-dashboard"]),
515: )
516: ```
517: 
518: `only_accessed()` is order-dependent. If you call it before accessing any flags with `is_enabled()` or `get_flag()`, no feature flag properties are attached.
519: 
520: #### Method 2: Include the `$feature/feature_flag_name` property manually
521: 
522: In the event properties, include `$feature/feature_flag_name: variant_key`:
523: 
524: ```python
525: posthog.capture(
526:     "event_name",
527:     distinct_id="distinct_id_of_the_user",
528:     properties={
529:         # Replace feature-flag-key with your flag key and "variant-key" with the key of your variant
530:         "$feature/feature-flag-key": "variant-key",
531:     },
532: )
533: ```
534: 
535: ### Evaluating only specific flags
536: 
537: By default, `posthog.evaluate_flags()` evaluates every flag for the user. If you only need a few flags, pass `flag_keys` to request only those flags:
538: 
539: ```python
540: flags = posthog.evaluate_flags(
541:     "distinct_id_of_your_user",
542:     flag_keys=["checkout-flow", "new-dashboard"],
543: )
544: ```
545: 
546: ### Sending `$feature_flag_called` events
547: 
548: Capturing `$feature_flag_called` events enables PostHog to know when a flag was accessed by a user and provide [analytics and insights](https://posthog.com/docs/product-analytics/insights.md) on the flag. With `posthog.evaluate_flags()`, the SDK sends this event when you call `flags.is_enabled()` or `flags.get_flag()` for a flag.
549: 
550: The SDK deduplicates these events per `(distinct_id, flag, value)` in a local cache. If you reinitialize the PostHog client, the cache resets and `$feature_flag_called` events may be sent again. PostHog handles duplicates, so duplicate `$feature_flag_called` events don't affect your analytics.
551: 
552: `flags.get_flag_payload()` doesn't send `$feature_flag_called` events and doesn't count as an access for `only_accessed()`.
553: 
554: ### Advanced: Overriding server properties
555: 
556: Sometimes, you may want to evaluate feature flags using [person properties](https://posthog.com/docs/product-analytics/person-properties.md), [groups](https://posthog.com/docs/product-analytics/group-analytics.md), or group properties that haven't been ingested yet, or were set incorrectly earlier.
557: 
558: You can provide properties to evaluate the flag with by using the `person properties`, `groups`, and `group properties` arguments. PostHog will then use these values to evaluate the flag, instead of any properties currently stored on your PostHog server.
559: 
560: For example:
561: 
562: ```python
563: flags = posthog.evaluate_flags(
564:     "distinct_id_of_the_user",
565:     person_properties={"property_name": "value"},
566:     groups={
567:         "your_group_type": "your_group_id",
568:         "another_group_type": "your_group_id",
569:     },
570:     group_properties={
571:         "your_group_type": {"group_property_name": "value"},
572:         "another_group_type": {"group_property_name": "value"},
573:     },
574: )
575: 
576: if flags.is_enabled("flag-key"):
577:     # Do something differently for this user
578: ```
579: 
580: ### Overriding GeoIP properties
581: 
582: By default, a user's GeoIP properties are set using the IP address they use to capture events on the frontend. You may want to override the these properties when evaluating feature flags. A common reason to do this is when you're not using PostHog on your frontend, so the user has no GeoIP properties.
583: 
584: You can override GeoIP properties by including them in the `person_properties` parameter when evaluating feature flags. This is useful when you're evaluating flags on your backend and want to use the client's location instead of your server's location.
585: 
586: The following GeoIP properties can be overridden:
587: 
588: -   `$geoip_country_code`
589: -   `$geoip_country_name`
590: -   `$geoip_city_name`
591: -   `$geoip_city_confidence`
592: -   `$geoip_continent_code`
593: -   `$geoip_continent_name`
594: -   `$geoip_latitude`
595: -   `$geoip_longitude`
596: -   `$geoip_postal_code`
597: -   `$geoip_subdivision_1_code`
598: -   `$geoip_subdivision_1_name`
599: -   `$geoip_subdivision_2_code`
600: -   `$geoip_subdivision_2_name`
601: -   `$geoip_subdivision_3_code`
602: -   `$geoip_subdivision_3_name`
603: -   `$geoip_time_zone`
604: 
605: Simply include any of these properties in the `person_properties` parameter alongside your other person properties when calling feature flags.
606: 
607: ### Request timeout
608: 
609: You can configure the `feature_flags_request_timeout_seconds` parameter when initializing your PostHog client to set a flag request timeout. This helps prevent your code from being blocked if PostHog's servers are too slow to respond. By default, this is set to 3 seconds.
610: 
611: ```python
612: posthog = Posthog(
613:     "<ph_project_token>",
614:     host="https://us.i.posthog.com",
615:     feature_flags_request_timeout_seconds=3,  # Time in seconds. Defaults to 3.
616: )
617: ```
618: 
619: ### Local evaluation
620: 
621: Evaluating feature flags requires making a request to PostHog for each flag. However, you can improve performance by evaluating flags locally. Instead of making a request for each flag, PostHog will periodically request and store feature flag definitions locally, enabling you to evaluate flags without making additional requests.
622: 
623: It is best practice to use local evaluation flags when possible, since this enables you to resolve flags faster and with fewer API calls.
624: 
625: For details on how to implement local evaluation, see our [local evaluation guide](https://posthog.com/docs/feature-flags/local-evaluation.md).
626: 
627: #### Distributed environments
628: 
629: In multi-worker or edge environments, you can implement custom caching for flag definitions using Redis, Cloudflare KV, or other storage backends. This enables sharing definitions across workers and coordinating fetches. See our guide for [local evaluation in distributed environments](https://posthog.com/docs/feature-flags/local-evaluation/distributed-environments?tab=Python.md) for details.

683: ## Distributed tracing
684: 
685: > Requires `posthog` version 7.58.0 or later.
686: 
687: **The span API is experimental**
688: 
689: Tracing is new in the Python SDK and its API can still change in a minor release. Spans you send are kept – it's the SDK surface that isn't frozen yet.
690: 
691: Tracing records **spans** – timed units of work – so you can see where time went in a request and how work fans out across your services. Spans created inside a [context](#contexts) automatically carry the person and session they belong to, so a slow trace links back to the person who experienced it.
692: 
693: Tracing is off until you set the `traces` option. No OpenTelemetry dependency is required. For what you can do with spans once they arrive, see [Distributed tracing](https://posthog.com/docs/distributed-tracing/start-here.md).
694: 
695: ```python
696: from posthog import Posthog
697: 
698: posthog = Posthog(
699:     "<ph_project_token>",
700:     host="https://us.i.posthog.com",
701:     traces={"service_name": "checkout-api"},
702: )
703: ```
704: 
705: If you use the module-level API instead, set `posthog.traces = {"service_name": "checkout-api"}` alongside your other options, before you start the first span.
706: 
707: Set `service_name` – PostHog groups operations by service and span name.
708: 
709: Tracing is available on the synchronous `Posthog` client and the module-level API. `AsyncPosthog` doesn't support it yet.
710: 
711: ### Creating spans
712: 
713: `start_span` returns a span. Use it in a `with` block to make it the active span for the block and end it when the block exits. Spans started inside the block nest underneath it automatically.
714: 
715: ```python
716: with posthog.start_span("POST /checkout", kind="server") as span:
717:     span.set_attribute("plan", user.plan)
718: 
719:     with posthog.start_span("create-order"):
720:         order = create_order(cart)
721:     with posthog.start_span("charge-card"):
722:         stripe.charge(order)
723: ```
724: 
725: If an exception escapes the block, the span records it, its status is set to `error`, and the exception propagates unchanged. `KeyboardInterrupt`, `GeneratorExit`, and `asyncio.CancelledError` still end the span but aren't recorded as failures.
726: 
727: The recorded exception includes the stack trace, which contains file paths from your server. If you'd rather those didn't leave your process, remove `exception.stacktrace` in [`before_span_send`](#scrubbing-and-dropping-spans).
728: 
729: For work that can't wrap a block, call `start_span` without `with`. **A span started this way isn't active**, so spans started afterwards aren't its children unless you pass `parent` explicitly – and you must call `end()` yourself.
730: 
731: ```python
732: span = posthog.start_span("background-sync", attributes={"queue": "emails"})
733: try:
734:     # Explicitly parent a child to a span that isn't active.
735:     child = posthog.start_span("send-batch", parent=span)
736:     child.end()
737: finally:
738:     span.end()
739: ```
740: 
741: `get_active_span()` returns the span active in the current context, or `None` when there isn't one.
742: 
743: The active span is tracked with [`contextvars`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/contextvars.html), so it carries across `await` in asyncio code. Threads don't reliably inherit it – pass `parent=span` to continue the trace in a thread you start or a `ThreadPoolExecutor` task. A forked child process starts with no active span, so pass `parent` there too.
744: 
745: `start_span` always returns a usable span, even when tracing is off, so your code never needs to check whether tracing is enabled.
746: 
747: ### Span names and attributes
748: 
749: Span names should be low-cardinality operation names – `GET /users/:id`, not `GET /users/123`. Variable values belong in attributes. Strings, booleans, integers, and floats keep their type. Lists and dictionaries are sent as arrays and maps, but PostHog stores them as serialized strings. Setting an attribute to `None` removes it, and any other value is converted to a string.
750: 
751: ```python
752: with posthog.start_span("GET /users/:id", kind="server") as span:
753:     span.set_attributes({"user.id": user_id, "db.rows": len(rows)})
754:     span.add_event("cache-miss")
755: 
756:     if not rows:
757:         span.set_status("error", "user not found")
758: ```
759: 
760: | Method | Description |
761: | --- | --- |
762: | `set_attribute(key, value)` | Set a single attribute |
763: | `set_attributes(attributes)` | Merge several attributes at once |
764: | `add_event(name, attributes=None, timestamp=None)` | Record a timestamped event within the span |
765: | `set_status(code, message=None)` | Set the outcome: `"ok"` or `"error"`. `"ok"` is final – an exception raised later in the `with` block doesn't override it |
766: | `record_exception(exception)` | Attach an exception event carrying the type, message, and – for a raised exception – stack trace, and set status to `error`. Use it for exceptions you catch and handle |
767: | `update_name(name)` | Replace the span name, e.g. once a route template resolves |
768: | `traceparent()` | This span's W3C `traceparent` header value, or `None` |
769: | `tracestate()` | This span's W3C `tracestate` value, or `None` when it has none |
770: | `end(end_time=None)` | End the span and queue it for export. A `with` block does this for you |
771: 
772: Every method except `traceparent()`, `tracestate()`, and `end()` returns the span, so calls chain. Calls after `end()` are ignored.
773: 
774: `start_span` takes these keyword arguments:
775: 
776: | Argument | Description |
777: | --- | --- |
778: | `kind` | What the work is: `"internal"` (default), `"server"` for an inbound request, `"client"` for an outbound call, `"producer"` or `"consumer"` for queue work |
779: | `attributes` | Attributes to set at span start |
780: | `parent` | A span, or an inbound W3C `traceparent` string to continue a trace another service started. Defaults to the active span |
781: | `tracestate` | The W3C `tracestate` accompanying a `traceparent` string. Ignored when `parent` is a span, which inherits its parent's |
782: | `start_time` | Backdate the span's start, as a `datetime` or seconds since the epoch. The server clamps a start more than 24 hours old to receive time; with `debug` on, the SDK prints a debug message when you pass one |
783: 
784: ### Tracing across services
785: 
786: Spans use [W3C Trace Context](https://www.w3.org/TR/trace-context/), so a trace can span several services. Pass an inbound `traceparent` header as `parent` to continue a trace another service started, and send `span.traceparent()` onward when you call out.
787: 
788: app.py
789: 
790: ```python
791: import requests
792: from flask import request
793: 
794: 
795: @app.post("/checkout")
796: def checkout():
797:     with posthog.start_span(
798:         "POST /checkout",
799:         kind="server",
800:         parent=request.headers.get("traceparent"),
801:     ) as span:
802:         traceparent = span.traceparent()
803: 
804:         requests.post(
805:             "https://payments.internal/charge",
806:             headers={"traceparent": traceparent} if traceparent else {},
807:         )
808: 
809:         return {"status": "ok"}
810: ```
811: 
812: A malformed `traceparent` starts a new trace rather than raising. A missing one (`None`) falls back to the active span, if there is one.
813: 
814: A continued trace propagates the sampled flag it was handed, so a downstream sampler sees the decision the head service made. PostHog itself doesn't sample – a span is recorded and exported whichever way that flag is set.
815: 
816: ### Linking traces to people and sessions
817: 
818: Spans created inside a [context](#contexts) that has a distinct ID or session ID automatically carry `posthogDistinctId` and `sessionId` attributes, which is what makes a trace reachable from a person or a Session Replay recording. In Django, the [contexts middleware](https://posthog.com/docs/libraries/django.md#django-contexts-middleware) sets these for every request. Elsewhere, set them yourself:
819: 
820: ```python
821: from posthog import new_context, identify_context, set_context_session
822: 
823: with new_context():
824:     identify_context(user.id)
825:     set_context_session(session_id)
826: 
827:     with posthog.start_span("POST /checkout"):
828:         process_order()
829: ```
830: 
831: Spans created outside a context with those values omit the attributes.
832: 
833: ### Scrubbing and dropping spans
834: 
835: `before_span_send` runs on every finished span before it's queued for export. It receives the span as a dict with `name`, `kind`, `status`, `attributes`, `events`, `start_time_ns`, `end_time_ns`, `trace_id`, `span_id`, and `parent_span_id`. Edit it and return it, or return `None` to drop the span entirely.
836: 
837: ```python
838: def scrub_spans(span):
839:     if span["attributes"].get("http.route") == "/health":
840:         return None
841: 
842:     span["attributes"].pop("http.request.header.authorization", None)
843:     return span
844: 
845: 
846: posthog = Posthog(
847:     "<ph_project_token>",
848:     host="https://us.i.posthog.com",
849:     traces={
850:         "service_name": "checkout-api",
851:         "before_span_send": scrub_spans,
852:     },
853: )
854: ```
855: 
856: Attributes are plain Python values, not the OTLP wire encoding. The hook runs after PostHog attaches `posthogDistinctId` and `sessionId`, so those are visible to the hook and can be scrubbed too. An exception's stack trace is on its event, under `event["attributes"]["exception.stacktrace"]`.
857: 
858: -   `trace_id`, `span_id`, and `parent_span_id` are read-only. Rewriting them would orphan child spans that have already been exported, so changes are reverted.
859: -   A hook that raises drops the span rather than exporting it without scrubbing.
860: -   Pass a list to run several hooks in order. The first one to return `None` stops the chain.
861: -   The hook must be a regular function. An `async` hook drops every span.
862: -   If an entry isn't callable, tracing turns off for the client rather than exporting spans the hook was meant to scrub.
863: 
864: ### Span limits
865: 
866: A span is capped at 128 attributes and 128 events, each event at 128 attributes, and each string attribute value at 8192 characters. The endpoint rejects a span that's too large, and a rejected span is lost whole rather than truncated, so the caps bound a span before it gets there.
867: 
868: Past the cap, the earliest attributes and events are kept and the number dropped is reported alongside the span, so a truncated span reads as truncated rather than as quietly incomplete. The attributes PostHog attaches itself – `posthogDistinctId` and `sessionId` – don't count toward the cap and are never dropped, so a span at the limit still links back to its person and session.
869: 
870: The event cap is absolute: an `exception` event the SDK records for you spends an ordinary slot like any other. A span that fills its events and then raises keeps its `error` status but not the exception detail, and reports the loss as a dropped event. Raise `max_events_per_span` on spans that record many events and can also fail.
871: 
872: The length bound reaches inside a value, including strings nested in lists and dictionaries, and applies to `exception.stacktrace` like any other attribute – a long stack trace keeps its last 8192 characters. All four caps are re-applied after `before_span_send`, so a hook that enriches a span can't push it back over.
873: 
874: ### Configuration
875: 
876: | Option | Default | Description |
877: | --- | --- | --- |
878: | `service_name` | – | Name of the service producing spans. Set this |
879: | `service_version` | – | Version of the service |
880: | `environment` | – | Deployment environment, e.g. `production` |
881: | `resource_attributes` | – | Extra OTLP resource attributes. Takes precedence over the fields above |
882: | `flush_interval` | `5` | Seconds between exports of queued spans |
883: | `max_export_batch_size` | `512` | Maximum spans per request |
884: | `max_queue_size` | `2048` | Maximum spans held in memory. Spans beyond this are dropped |
885: | `max_live_spans` | `10000` | Maximum spans open at once. At the limit `start_span` returns a span that isn't recorded |
886: | `max_span_age` | `3600` | Once `max_live_spans` is reached, spans open longer than this many seconds are treated as leaked and never exported |
887: | `before_span_send` | – | Edit or drop each finished span before export. Return `None` to drop it |
888: | `max_attributes_per_span` | `128` | Maximum attributes you set on one span |
889: | `max_events_per_span` | `128` | Maximum events on one span |
890: | `max_attribute_value_length` | `8192` | Maximum characters in a string attribute value |
891: 
892: An invalid value falls back to its default with a warning. The exception is `before_span_send`: an entry that isn't callable turns tracing off.
893: 
894: ### Shutdown and short-lived processes
895: 
896: Spans are exported on a background interval, even with `sync_mode` on. Both `flush()` and `shutdown()` export spans that have already ended. A span still open at `flush()` is exported once it ends; a span still open at `shutdown()` is discarded with a warning, so end your spans before shutting down – a `with` block does this for you. `shutdown()` gives queued spans up to 30 seconds to send.
897: 
898: If your serverless handler reuses a client across invocations, call `flush()` before returning. It flushes events and ended spans concurrently without stopping the client. Reserve `shutdown()` for a disposable client or process exit.
899: 
900: ```python
901: def handler(event, context):
902:     try:
903:         with posthog.start_span("handler"):
904:             do_work()
905:     finally:
906:         posthog.flush()
907: ```
908: 
909: A script that exits without calling `shutdown()` still gets a brief best-effort flush at exit, but don't rely on it for spans you need.
910: 
911: ## GeoIP properties
912: 
913: Before posthog-python v3.0, we added GeoIP properties to all incoming events by default. We also used these properties for feature flag evaluation, based on the IP address of the request. This isn't ideal since they are created based on your server IP address, rather than the user's, leading to incorrect location resolution.
914: 
915: As of posthog-python v3.0, the default now is to disregard the server IP, not add the GeoIP properties, and not use the values for feature flag evaluations.
916: 
917: You can go back to previous behavior by doing setting the `disable_geoip` argument in your initialization to `False`:
918: 
919: ```python
920: posthog = Posthog('api_key', disable_geoip=False)
921: ```
922: 
923: The list of properties that this overrides:
924: 
925: 1.  `$geoip_city_name`
926: 2.  `$geoip_country_name`
927: 3.  `$geoip_country_code`
928: 4.  `$geoip_continent_name`
929: 5.  `$geoip_continent_code`
930: 6.  `$geoip_postal_code`
931: 7.  `$geoip_time_zone`
932: 
933: You can also explicitly chose to enable or disable GeoIP for a single capture request like so:
934: 
935: ```python
936: posthog.capture('test_event', disable_geoip=True|False)
937: ```
938: 
939: ## Debug mode
940: 
941: If you're not seeing the expected events being captured, the feature flags being evaluated, or the surveys being shown, you can enable debug mode to see what's happening.
942: 
943: You can enable debug mode by setting the `debug` option to `True` in the `PostHog` object. This will enable verbose logs about the inner workings of the SDK.
944: 
945: ```python
946: posthog.debug = True
947: ```
948: 
949: ## Disabling requests during tests
950: 
951: You can disable requests during tests by setting the `disabled` option to `True` in the `PostHog` object. This means no events will be captured or no requests will be sent to PostHog.
952: 
953: ```python
954: if settings.TEST:
955:     posthog.disabled = True
956: ```
957: 
958: ## Connection configuration
959: 
960: The SDK uses HTTP connection pooling internally for better performance. These settings typically need not be changed, but in some environments, such as when running behind NAT gateways, pooled connections may be terminated non-gracefully, causing request failures.
961: 
962: You can configure connection behavior in several ways. The following settings should be called during initialization, before any API requests are made.
963: 
964: ### Enable TCP keepalive
965: 
966: TCP keepalive probes help prevent idle connections from being dropped by network infrastructure. This is the recommended approach for most cases where idle connections are terminated.
967: 
968: ```python
969: import posthog
970: 
971: posthog.enable_keep_alive()
972: ```
973: 
974: This enables TCP keepalive with sensible defaults (60 second idle time, 60 second probe interval, 3 probes before timeout).
975: 
976: ### Disable connection pooling
977: 
978: If you need each request to use a fresh connection, you can disable connection reuse entirely. This will incur additional overhead per request but may be desirable in some circumstances.
979: 
980: ```python
981: import posthog
982: 
983: posthog.disable_connection_reuse()
984: ```
985: 
986: ### Custom HTTP socket options
987: 
988: For advanced use cases, you can configure arbitrary socket options on the underlying HTTP connection.
989: 
990: ```python
991: import socket
992: import posthog
993: 
994: posthog.set_socket_options([
995:     (socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_KEEPALIVE, 1),
996:     # Add additional socket options as needed
997: ])
998: ```
999: 
1000: Pass `None` to `set_socket_options()` to reset to default behavior.
1001: 
1002: ## Filtering or modifying events before sending
1003: 
1004: Use `before_send` to modify or drop events before they are queued for delivery. Return the modified event dictionary to send it, or `None` to drop it.
1005: 
1006: ```python
1007: from typing import Any
1008: 
1009: import posthog
1010: 
1011: 
1012: def scrub_pii(event: dict[str, Any]) -> dict[str, Any] | None:
1013:     properties = event.get("properties", {})
1014: 
1015:     if "email" in properties:
1016:         email = properties["email"]
1017:         properties["email"] = f"***@{email.split('@', 1)[1]}" if "@" in email else "***"
1018: 
1019:     if event.get("event") == "test_event":
1020:         return None
1021: 
1022:     return event
1023: 
1024: 
1025: client = posthog.Client(
1026:     "<ph_project_api_key>",
1027:     before_send=scrub_pii,
1028: )
1029: ```
1030: 
1031: If your callback raises an exception, the SDK logs the error and continues with the original unmodified event.
1032: 
1033: ## Historical migrations
1034: 
1035: You can use the Python or Node SDK to run [historical migrations](https://posthog.com/docs/migrate.md) of data into PostHog. To do so, set the `historical_migration` option to `true` when initializing the client.
1036: 
1037: ### Python
1038: 
1039: ```python
1040: from posthog import Posthog
1041: from datetime import datetime
1042: 
1043: posthog = Posthog(
1044:     '<ph_project_token>',
1045:     host='https://us.i.posthog.com',
1046:     debug=True,
1047:     historical_migration=True
1048: )
1049: 
1050: events = [
1051:   {
1052:     "event": "batched_event_name",
1053:     "distinct_id": "user_id",
1054:     "timestamp": datetime.fromisoformat("2024-04-02T12:00:00+00:00"),
1055:     "properties": {"account_type": "pro"}
1056:   },
1057:   {
1058:     "event": "batched_event_name",
1059:     "distinct_id": "user_id",
1060:     "timestamp": datetime.fromisoformat("2024-04-03T09:30:00+00:00"),
1061:     "properties": {"account_type": "pro"}
1062:   }
1063: ]
1064: 
1065: for event in events:
1066:   posthog.capture(
1067:     event["event"],
1068:     distinct_id=event["distinct_id"],
1069:     properties=event["properties"],
1070:     timestamp=event["timestamp"],
1071:   )
1072: 
1073: posthog.shutdown()
1074: ```
1075: 
1076: ### Node.js
1077: 
1078: ```javascript
1079: import { PostHog } from 'posthog-node'
1080: 
1081: const client = new PostHog(
1082:     '<ph_project_token>',
1083:     {
1084:       host: 'https://us.i.posthog.com',
1085:       historicalMigration: true
1086:     }
1087: )
1088: 
1089: client.debug()
1090: 
1091: client.capture({
1092:     event: "batched_event_name",
1093:     distinctId: "user_id",
1094:     properties: {},
1095:     timestamp: new Date("2024-04-03T12:00:00Z")
1096: })
1097: 
1098: client.capture({
1099:     event: "batched_event_name",
1100:     distinctId: "user_id",
1101:     properties: {},
1102:     timestamp: new Date("2024-04-03T13:00:00Z")
1103: })
1104: 
1105: await client.shutdown()
1106: ```
1107: 
1108: ## Serverless environments (Render/Lambda/...)
1109: 
1110: ### Synchronous `Posthog`
1111: 
1112: By default, the synchronous `Posthog` client buffers events before sending them to the capture endpoint. A serverless platform can freeze or terminate the runtime before background delivery finishes.
1113: 
1114: -   For a client shared across invocations, call `posthog.flush()` before the handler returns, including when application code throws. This blocking call attempts to deliver queued events without stopping the client. Its `timeout_seconds` argument defaults to `10` seconds.
1115: -   For a disposable client or process exit, call `posthog.shutdown()` after its final work. It attempts to deliver queued events and cleans up the client. Don't reuse the client afterward. Unlike Node's `shutdown()`, Python's `shutdown()` takes no timeout argument.
1116: -   Alternatively, enable `sync_mode` when initializing the client so each `posthog.capture()` call attempts delivery before it returns.
1117: 
1118: These calls do not guarantee that PostHog received every event. If you use [distributed tracing](#distributed-tracing), `sync_mode` doesn't apply to spans. For a shared client, call `posthog.flush()` before the handler returns – see [Shutdown and short-lived processes](#shutdown-and-short-lived-processes).
1119: 
1120: ### Asyncio `AsyncPosthog`
1121: 
1122: Keep one `AsyncPosthog` client for the lifetime of your application. Use buffered `capture()` by default, or `await capture_immediate()` when one invocation must wait for an event's delivery attempt. Call `await posthog.shutdown()` once during application cleanup. Don't shut down the client after each request.
1123: 
1124: ## Django
1125: 
1126: See our [Django docs](https://posthog.com/docs/libraries/django.md) for how to set up PostHog in Django. The [Django contexts middleware](https://posthog.com/docs/libraries/django.md#django-contexts-middleware) adds request properties and authenticated user identity to events captured during a request. You can also opt in to browser session and distinct ID headers.
1127: 
1128: ## ASGI request middleware
1129: 
1130: Version `7.69.0` and later of the Python SDK includes framework-independent ASGI middleware for FastAPI, Starlette, Litestar, and raw ASGI applications. It creates a PostHog context for each HTTP or WebSocket request, enriches captured events with request properties, and captures exceptions that escape the application.
1131: 
1132: For FastAPI or Starlette, add the middleware to your app:
1133: 
1134: ```python
1135: from fastapi import FastAPI
1136: from posthog import Posthog
1137: from posthog.integrations.asgi import PosthogASGIMiddleware
1138: 
1139: posthog = Posthog(
1140:     "<ph_project_token>",
1141:     host="https://us.i.posthog.com",
1142:     enable_exception_autocapture=True,
1143: )
1144: 
1145: app = FastAPI()
1146: app.add_middleware(PosthogASGIMiddleware, client=posthog)
1147: ```
1148: 
1149: The middleware's `capture_exceptions` option defaults to `None`, which inherits the client's `enable_exception_autocapture` setting. Set it to `True` or `False` to override the client. Use `request_filter` to skip selected requests and `extra_properties` to add properties from the ASGI scope. Both callbacks can be synchronous or asynchronous.
1150: 
1151: The middleware ignores `X-PostHog-Distinct-ID` and `X-PostHog-Session-ID` by default because clients can control them. Set `trust_tracing_headers=True` only when you want to accept these headers as analytics context. Don't use them for authentication or authorization.

3: # Identify users
4: 
5: Canonical URL: https://posthog.com/docs/getting-started/identify-users
6: 
7: > **Cloud region:** This page uses US Cloud hosts. For an EU Cloud project, use `https://eu.i.posthog.com` instead of `https://us.i.posthog.com` (ingestion host).
8: 
9: ## On this page
10: 
11: - [How identify works](#how-identify-works)
12: - [Best practices when using identify](#best-practices-when-using-identify)
13: - [Further reading](#further-reading)
14: 
15: Linking events to specific users enables you to build a full picture of how they're using your product across different sessions, devices, and platforms.
16: 
17: This is straightforward to do when [capturing backend events](https://posthog.com/docs/product-analytics/capture-events?tab=Node.js.md), as you associate events to a specific user using a `distinct_id`, which is a required argument.
18: 
19: However, in the frontend of a [web](https://posthog.com/docs/libraries/js/usage.md#capturing-events) or [mobile app](https://posthog.com/docs/libraries/ios.md#capturing-events), a `distinct_id` is not a required argument — PostHog's SDKs will generate an anonymous `distinct_id` for you automatically and you can capture events anonymously, provided you use the appropriate [configuration](https://posthog.com/docs/libraries/js/usage.md#capturing-anonymous-events).
20: 
21: To link events to specific users, call `identify`:
22: 
23: ### Web
24: 
25: ```javascript
26: posthog.identify(
27:   'distinct_id',  // Replace 'distinct_id' with your user's unique identifier
28:   { email: 'max@hedgehogmail.com', name: 'Max Hedgehog' } // optional: set additional person properties
29: );
30: ```
31: 
32: ### Android
33: 
34: ```kotlin
35: PostHog.identify(
36:     distinctId = distinctID, // Replace 'distinctID' with your user's unique identifier
37:     // optional: set additional person properties
38:     userProperties = mapOf(
39:         "name" to "Max Hedgehog",
40:         "email" to "max@hedgehogmail.com"
41:     )
42: )
43: ```
44: 
45: ### iOS
46: 
47: ```swift
48: PostHogSDK.shared.identify("distinct_id", // Replace "distinct_id" with your user's unique identifier
49:                            userProperties: ["name": "Max Hedgehog", "email": "max@hedgehogmail.com"]) // optional: set additional person properties
50: ```
51: 
52: ### React Native
53: 
54: ```jsx
55: posthog.identify('distinct_id', { // Replace "distinct_id" with your user's unique identifier
56:     email: 'max@hedgehogmail.com', // optional: set additional person properties
57:     name: 'Max Hedgehog'
58: })
59: ```
60: 
61: ### Dart
62: 
63: ```dart
64: await Posthog().identify(
65:   userId: 'distinct_id', // Replace "distinct_id" with your user's unique identifier
66:   userProperties: {
67:     'email': 'max@hedgehogmail.com', // optional: set additional person properties
68:     'name': 'Max Hedgehog',
69:   },
70: );
71: ```
72: 
73: Events captured after calling `identify` are identified events and this creates a person profile if one doesn't exist already.
74: 
75: Due to the cost of processing them, anonymous events can be up to 4x cheaper than identified events, so it's recommended you only capture identified events when needed.
76: 
77: ## How identify works
78: 
79: When a user starts browsing your website or app, PostHog automatically assigns them an **anonymous ID**, which is stored locally.
80: 
81: Provided you've [configured persistence](https://posthog.com/docs/libraries/js/persistence.md) to use cookies or `localStorage`, this enables us to track anonymous users – even across different sessions.
82: 
83: By calling `identify` with a `distinct_id` of your choice (usually the user's ID in your database, or their email), you link the anonymous ID and distinct ID together.
84: 
85: Thus, all past and future events made with that anonymous ID are now associated with the distinct ID.
86: 
87: This enables you to do things like associate events with a user from before they log in for the first time, or associate their events across different devices or platforms.
88: 
89: **Using identify in the backend**
90: 
91: Although you can call `identify` using our backend SDKs, it is used most in frontends. This is because there is no concept of anonymous sessions in the backend SDKs, so calling `identify` only updates person profiles.
92: 
93: ## Best practices when using `identify`
94: 
95: ### 1\. Call `identify` as soon as you're able to
96: 
97: In your frontend, you should call `identify` as soon as you're able to.
98: 
99: Typically, this is every time your **app loads** for the first time, and directly after your **users log in**.
100: 
101: This ensures that events sent during your users' sessions are correctly associated with them.
102: 
103: You only need to call `identify` once per session, and you should avoid calling it multiple times unnecessarily.
104: 
105: If you call `identify` multiple times with the same data without reloading the page in between, PostHog will ignore the subsequent calls.
106: 
107: #### Identify users when the web SDK loads
108: 
109: If your app already knows the signed-in user when you initialize the JavaScript web SDK, the [`loaded` callback](https://posthog.com/docs/libraries/js/config.md) is a convenient place to call `identify`. This identifies the user as soon as the SDK has loaded:
110: 
111: ```javascript
112: posthog.init('<ph_project_token>', {
113:     api_host: 'https://us.i.posthog.com',
114:     defaults: '2026-05-30',
115:     loaded: (posthog) => {
116:         if (currentUser?.id) {
117:             posthog.identify(currentUser.id, {
118:                 email: currentUser.email,
119:                 name: currentUser.name,
120:             })
121:         }
122:     },
123: })
124: ```
125: 
126: In this example, `currentUser` represents user data already available from your authentication system. If your app loads the user asynchronously, call `posthog.identify()` as soon as that data becomes available instead.
127: 
128: ### 2\. Use unique strings for distinct IDs
129: 
130: If two users have the same distinct ID, their data is merged and they are considered one user in PostHog. Two common ways this can happen are:
131: 
132: -   Your logic for generating IDs does not generate sufficiently strong IDs and you can end up with a clash where 2 users have the same ID.
133: -   There's a bug, typo, or mistake in your code leading to most or all users being identified with generic IDs like `null`, `true`, or `distinctId`.
134: 
135: PostHog also has built-in protections to stop the most common distinct ID mistakes.
136: 
137: ### 3\. Reset after logout
138: 
139: If a user logs out on your frontend, you should call `reset()` to unlink any future events made on that device with that user.
140: 
141: This is important if your users are sharing a computer, as otherwise all of those users are grouped together into a single user due to shared cookies between sessions.
142: 
143: **We strongly recommend you call `reset` on logout even if you don't expect users to share a computer.**
144: 
145: You can do that like so:
146: 
147: ### Web
148: 
149: ```javascript
150: posthog.reset()
151: ```
152: 
153: ### iOS
154: 
155: ```swift
156: PostHogSDK.shared.reset()
157: ```
158: 
159: ### Android
160: 
161: ```kotlin
162: PostHog.reset()
163: ```
164: 
165: ### React Native
166: 
167: ```jsx
168: posthog.reset()
169: ```
170: 
171: ### Dart
172: 
173: ```dart
174: await Posthog().reset();
175: ```
176: 
177: If you *also* want to reset the `device_id` so that the device will be considered a new device in future events, you can pass `true` as an argument:
178: 
179: ```javascript
180: posthog.reset(true)
181: ```
182: 
183: ### 4\. Person profiles and properties
184: 
185: You'll notice that one of the parameters in the `identify` method is a `properties` object.
186: 
187: This enables you to set [person properties](https://posthog.com/docs/product-analytics/person-properties.md).
188: 
189: Whenever possible, we recommend passing in all person properties you have available each time you call identify, as this ensures their person profile on PostHog is up to date.
190: 
191: Person properties can also be set being adding a `$set` property to a event `capture` call.
192: 
193: **`$set` and `$set_once` aren't stored on events**
194: 
195: These properties only tell PostHog how to update person data during ingestion — they aren't kept on the stored event, so you can't filter, break down, or query events by them. To query the values you set, use [person properties](https://posthog.com/docs/product-analytics/person-properties.md) instead.
196: 
197: See our [person properties docs](https://posthog.com/docs/product-analytics/person-properties.md) for more details on how to work with them and best practices.
198: 
199: ### 5\. Use deep links between platforms
200: 
201: We recommend you call `identify` [as soon as you're able](#1-call-identify-as-soon-as-youre-able), typically when a user signs up or logs in.
202: 
203: This doesn't work if one or both platforms are unauthenticated. Some examples of such cases are:
204: 
205: -   Onboarding and signup flows before authentication.
206: -   Unauthenticated web pages redirecting to authenticated mobile apps.
207: -   Authenticated web apps prompting an app download.
208: 
209: In these cases, you can use a [deep link](https://developer.android.com/training/app-links/deep-linking) on Android and [universal links](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/xcode/supporting-universal-links-in-your-app) on iOS to identify users.
210: 
211: 1.  Use `posthog.get_distinct_id()` to get the current distinct ID. Even if you cannot call identify because the user is unauthenticated, this will return an anonymous distinct ID generated by PostHog.
212: 2.  Add the distinct ID to the deep link as query parameters, along with other properties like UTM parameters.
213: 3.  When the user is redirected to the app, parse the deep link and handle the following cases:
214: 
215: -   The mobile app is already authenticated. In this case, call [`posthog.alias()`](https://posthog.com/docs/libraries/js/usage.md#alias) with the distinct ID from the web. This associates the two distinct IDs as a single person.
216: -   The mobile app is unauthenticated. In this case, call [`posthog.identify()`](https://posthog.com/docs/libraries/js/usage.md#identifying-users) with the distinct ID from the web so pre-login mobile events stay connected to the web session. When the user later logs in on mobile, call `identify()` again with your canonical user ID.
217: 
218: As long as you associate the distinct IDs with `posthog.identify()` or `posthog.alias()`, you can track events generated across platforms.
219: 
220: Here's an example implementation for handling deep links from web to mobile:
221: 
222: ### iOS
223: 
224: ```swift
225: import PostHog
226: 
227: class DeepLinkIdentityManager {
228:     static let shared = DeepLinkIdentityManager()
229: 
230:     // MARK: - Deep Link Received
231: 
232:     func handleDeepLink(_ url: URL, isAuthenticatedOnMobile: Bool) {
233:         guard let webDistinctId = URLComponents(url: url, resolvingAgainstBaseURL: true)?
234:             .queryItems?.first(where: { $0.name == "ph_distinct_id" })?.value else {
235:             return
236:         }
237: 
238:         if isAuthenticatedOnMobile {
239:             // The mobile app already knows the current user.
240:             // Alias the incoming web distinct ID to that user.
241:             PostHogSDK.shared.alias(webDistinctId)
242:         } else {
243:             // Reuse the web distinct ID until login on mobile.
244:             PostHogSDK.shared.identify(webDistinctId)
245:         }
246:     }
247:

1: # Deployment
2: 
3: ## Project Site (GitHub Pages)
4: 
5: The static site in `website/` is published to
6: **[https://alehar9320.github.io/agentic-odi/](https://alehar9320.github.io/agentic-odi/)**
7: by [`.github/workflows/pages.yml`](../.github/workflows/pages.yml).
8: 
9: - A push to `main` runs the website tests, builds `_site` from `website/`, and
10:   deploys the artifact with `actions/deploy-pages`.
11: - `workflow_dispatch` republishes the site from the Actions tab without a code
12:   change.
13: - Pages is configured with the "GitHub Actions" source, so there is no
14:   `gh-pages` branch. Removing `pages.yml` stops all publishing and the site
15:   returns 404.
16: - The `github-pages` environment only allows deployments from `main`.
17: 
18: ## Hosted MCP Server
19: 
20: The server is deployed via **[Horizon Prefect](https://www.prefect.io/horizon)**,
21: Prefect's managed infrastructure for hosting MCP-compatible agents.
22: 
23: ## Test Chat (UI)
24: 
25: Interact with the deployed agent directly in your browser:
26: 
27: > **[https://horizon.prefect.io/alhase/servers/agentic-odi/chat](https://horizon.prefect.io/alhase/servers/agentic-odi/chat)**
28: 
29: ## MCP Server Endpoint
30: 
31: Integrate via the MCP protocol at:
32: 
33: > **[https://agentic-odi.fastmcp.app/mcp](https://agentic-odi.fastmcp.app/mcp)**
34: 
35: > [!IMPORTANT]
36: > **Authentication is required** to access the MCP server endpoint. Please reach
37: > out to the maintainers to obtain the necessary credentials before connecting a
38: > client.
39: 
40: ## Hosted Studio
41: 
42: The Living Studio SPA is deployed to Cloudflare Workers:
43: 
44: | Environment | URL |
45: |---|---|
46: | Production (`main`) | **[https://agentic-odi.alehar.workers.dev/](https://agentic-odi.alehar.workers.dev/)** |
47: | Pull request preview | Posted automatically by Cloudflare Workers Builds as a PR comment |
48: 
49: Production deploys on every push to `main`. The Worker is `agentic-odi`; keep
50: `name` in `wrangler.jsonc` aligned with the Worker connected in the dashboard.
51: Preview builds run for non-production branches and are ephemeral: the Cloudflare
52: PR comment is the source of truth, so do not copy a preview URL into docs. The
53: hosted UI loads without a backend; canvas data, chat, and mutations need the
54: sidecar tunnel described below.
55: 
56: ## Living Studio on a Free Cloudflare Worker
57: 
58: Workers Containers — the only way to run the Python sidecar entirely on
59: Cloudflare — requires the Workers Paid plan. On the free plan, the Worker serves
60: the built SPA as Workers Static Assets and proxies `/api/*` to the sidecar
61: through a free, account-less
62: [Cloudflare Quick Tunnel](https://developers.cloudflare.com/tunnel/get-started/quick-tunnels/).
63: 
64: `wrangler.jsonc` publishes `apps/studio/dist` with SPA fallback and runs the Worker
65: first for `/api/*`; `infra/cloudflare/worker.ts` forwards those calls to the
66: `SIDECAR_URL` secret. The browser only talks to the Worker origin, so the
67: sidecar's CORS list is not involved.
68: 
69: ```bash
70: # 1. Build the SPA that the Worker uploads as static assets
71: npm --prefix apps/studio ci
72: npm --prefix apps/studio run build
73: 
74: # 2. Terminal A — MCP server (:8000) + sidecar (:8100)
75: python scripts/dev.py
76: 
77: # 3. Terminal B — free public URL for the sidecar (no account required)
78: cloudflared tunnel --url http://127.0.0.1:8100
79: # copy the https://<random>.trycloudflare.com URL it prints
80: 
81: # 4. Store the URL on the Worker, then deploy
82: npx wrangler secret put SIDECAR_URL   # paste the trycloudflare URL
83: npx wrangler deploy
84: ```
85: 
86: Workers Builds settings (Workers & Pages → your Worker → Settings → Builds):
87: 
88: | Setting | Value |
89: |---|---|
90: | Production branch | `main` |
91: | Root directory | `/` |
92: | Build command | `npm --prefix apps/studio ci && npm --prefix apps/studio run build` |
93: | Deploy command | `npx wrangler deploy` |
94: | Preview command | `npx wrangler preview` |
95: 
96: A Worker has no run command: the Worker script runs on Cloudflare. Set `name` in
97: `wrangler.jsonc` to the Worker you created before the first deploy.
98: 
99: ### Pull request previews
100: 
101: Workers Builds posts the build status and Preview URL to the pull request
102: automatically. To enable it:
103: 
104: 1. Open the Worker → **Settings** → **Build** → **Branch control**.
105: 2. Keep the production branch set to `main` and enable **Preview Builds**.
106: 3. If Cloudflare shows **Set up Worker Previews**, complete the one-time switch.
107:    This cannot be reversed.
108: 4. Confirm the Preview command is `npx wrangler preview`.
109: 
110: `wrangler.jsonc` must keep a `previews` block, even an empty one: the
111: `wrangler preview` command fails the build with "Your Wrangler configuration is
112: missing a `previews` block" without it. Assets and compatibility settings stay
113: at the top level, so `"previews": {}` is enough while Previews need no extra
114: settings. If a future Preview needs vars or bindings, add them under `previews`
115: with Preview-safe values.
116: 
117: Previews do not inherit production settings. The SPA loads from a Preview, but
118: `/api/*` returns `502 SIDECAR_URL is not configured` until a preview-specific
119: `SIDECAR_URL` secret is configured:
120: 
121: ```bash
122: npx wrangler preview secret put SIDECAR_URL --name <branch>
123: ```
124: 
125: When `--name` is omitted it defaults to the current git branch. Previews are
126: ephemeral, and pull requests from forks may not receive one. If Cloudflare does
127: not comment, paste the URL into the PR's **Deployment** section.
128: 
129: The `cf` CLI can inspect build triggers and recent builds (`cf builds triggers
130: list`, `cf builds list`) and create a Preview (`cf previews deploy`), but it does
131: not post GitHub PR comments. The Workers Builds Git integration owns the PR link;
132: `cf` is only an optional verification tool and requires `cf auth login`.
133: 
134: > [!NOTE]
135: > The sidecar runs on your machine, so the Worker only works while
136: > `python scripts/dev.py` and the Quick Tunnel are running. Quick Tunnel URLs
137: > change on every restart — update the secret with
138: > `npx wrangler secret put SIDECAR_URL`. Chat also needs a reachable
139: > OpenAI-compatible endpoint in the Studio's **Settings**; the canvas, job map,
140: > and impact simulation work without one.

(End of file - total 140 lines)
</content>
